entry.title: Godot Showcase - Sovereign Tower
entry.summary: Paul and Lisa from Wild Wits Games tell us about their experience working on Sovereign Tower.
entry.content:
Today, Paul Mozet (Lead Programmer on Sovereign Tower) and Lisa Garnier (Narrative Design and Technical Artist on Sovereign Tower) from Wild Wits Games tell us about their experience developing their latest Godot game: Sovereign Tower.

Sovereign Tower is a story-rich Round Table management RPG where you recruit eccentric Knights, assign quests and balance egos whilst carving out your kingdom’s destiny. The game is already out on Steam for Windows and Linux.

Can you tell us a little bit about your game?

Paul Mozet (Lead Programmer on Sovereign Tower): Sovereign Tower is a round table manager RPG, mostly narrative, where you are the new Sovereign of a kingdom. You will have to recruit knights at your round table and dispatch them through the kingdom to answer the grievances of your people and the other counties’ representatives that will come to see you, while managing the ego of all of those eccentric characters. And if anything goes awry, you can count on the demon of the tower to go back in time and try to handle things in a different way!

How did you get your start in game development? And how did it grow into a full-time position?

Paul: A composer friend of mine, Pierrick Veillerobe, motivated me to do a Ludum Dare game jam with him while I was studying computer science back in 2021. I loved the experience and we made a few more in the year after. At the same time, I had the opportunity to meet Corto and François, the founders of Wild Wits Games and they welcomed me in 2022 to do a two months internship as a programmer on Aetheris, the first game of the studio. As the internship went well, they offered me a full-time position at the studio, as a programmer, an offer that I immediately accepted.

Lisa Garnier (Narrative Design and Technical Artist on Sovereign Tower): I first started exploring interactive media while I was at art school, graduating in 2020. I then switched to a computer science program to develop more technical skills. Like Paul, I joined the team in 2023 after completing a few-month internship. For our previous projects, Aetheris and Crown Gambit, I worked in a technical art role, which suited me well given my background in art and computer science.
Sovereign Tower is the first project I’ve worked on as a narrative designer, which is something I’ve wanted to do for a long time!

What were some of the biggest challenges you faced during the development process, and how did you overcome them?

Paul: The biggest one I think about is the rewind mechanic. We needed to have two saves per played cycle, one for the morning and one for the afternoon, which should all remember the state of all previously played cycles. But it couldn’t be simple state saves as using the demon power is not simply going back to a previous state, as the Sovereign remembers all information they get. Add to that hundreds of narrative variables and quests and more than a hundred characters, and you’ll get the perfect bug factory! To overcome the issue, we split everything we needed to save as much as we could to be as precise as possible, and had to do a lot of testing. But even so, some issues slipped through at the release, which wasn’t a big surprise and we’re fixing those as fast as we can.

Lisa: When it comes to the story, one of our biggest challenges was keeping the scope under control in terms of word count and budget.
One of the things that makes Sovereign Tower so interesting and worth playing more than once is all the different ways the story can go, which play around with the time rewind mechanics. We always want to take these as far as we can to make the experience as interesting and cohesive as possible, but adding new time-rewind options to every little interaction just wasn’t realistic. Game localization is expensive, and as a small studio, every word counts. We spent ages talking about and rethinking our main story ideas, and once most of the content had been written, we had to cut out the extra bits: getting rid of some of the variations here and there and scaling back some of our ambitions, while making sure these changes weren’t too big to impact the player experience. It was a bit of a balancing act, and there were a few stressful moments during production when we really worried we’d have to throw away a lot of the story.

How did you come up with game design elements for your project, such as the time rewinding mechanic? Were there any game design changes based on iteration and playtesting?

Paul: The rewinding mechanic came up pretty early in the project conception, as we wanted to encourage players to explore the different narrative options the game was offering, so they would want to start a new playthrough right after finishing the first one. We already made a heavy narrative game with Crown Gambit, so we knew an incentive to dwell in the different paths would add a lot to the experience. For the rest of the core loop, it didn’t change a lot since the beginning of the conception to be honest. Of course, through playtesting we found a lot of quality of life features that we implemented, and others were requested by players and have been added in the game after the release. Also, even if we started working on Sovereign Tower before learning about the project, the release of Dispatch made us rethink a few things. The best example is the implementation of the level and experience system for the knights, which we felt was mandatory after finishing Dispatch. We also made a few adjustments to the knights’ tags system to make it more understandable.

How did you create the various character designs for your game? What were your sources of inspiration? How did you write character dialogues?

Lisa: Our art and creative director Gobert was often the starting point for our character designs from a visual perspective. He’s full of ideas and he’s always coming up with these really distinctive concepts he’s eager to explore, whether it’s more fantastical ideas like a wolf-knight inspired by the Beast of Gévaudan (Rufus) or a mermaid knight (Ligia), or more caricature-driven concepts, like the overworked salaryman (Oliver) or the insufferable rich kid (Gwendan).
His inspirations are pretty diverse, but there’s obviously a lot of medieval fantasy, pop culture, and Arthurian legend in the mix, which is also a big part of our fantasy world’s identity. These visual ideas often came together with character archetypes we wanted to explore, in terms of personality type: the shy one, the dominant one, the cursed one, and so on.
Early in development, we put together a huge collaborative board where we threw all kinds of ideas around, almost like a giant moodboard we could draw from later when fleshing out individual characters. We wanted each character to have a strong, immediately recognizable archetype, a bit like the cast of Ace Attorney, where every character has their own distinct personality and quirks.
It was a very collaborative process. While some characters were already clear from the start, others needed more discussion and refinement to make sure their characterisation felt in line with their design.
Once the characters were well-defined, with distinct personalities and clear character arcs, writing their dialogue was generally pretty straightforward and fun! Giving each of them their own way of speaking and little quirks also helped a lot, providing a clear direction and letting their voice naturally shape the writing. Of course, it still took a few iterations to get everything to the right level of quality, but overall, the process flowed really well, and bringing all these characters to life was a real pleasure.

In reviews, your game is regularly praised for its art direction. How did you handle the asset pipeline with Godot? Do you have any suggestions for improvement in this regard?

Lisa: For assets that were relatively straightforward to integrate (such as character portraits) Gobert would upload them to our repository and update them in Godot when needed. For more complex integrations (particularly UI elements) Paul or I would take over. Godot’s scene system made it really easy to organize and integrate assets, while also giving Gobert the flexibility to tweak and adjust things himself as we moved into the visual polish phase. This allowed him to iterate on the game’s visuals without having to go through a developer for every small change.
As for potential improvements, I don’t have any major suggestions based on our experience. The workflow felt intuitive for our needs, and overall the pipeline worked well for the scope of our project.

How did you animate scenes and UI elements in your project with Godot? What was your experience with Godot’s animation system, and do you have any ideas for improvement?

Lisa: We used a fairly even mix of AnimationPlayers and Tweens depending on the needs of each scene. I find both systems very complete and intuitive to work with, and I always enjoy writing a little tween with some juicy easing curves.
Animating UI nodes could be a bit tricky at the time as it often required little workarounds to animate them smoothly, given how constrained their transforms were by the UI layout system. Thankfully this became much easier with Godot 4.7 and the introduction of transform offsets making it far more straightforward to animate UI elements for small transitions.

How did you discover Godot? What made you pick it for your project?

Paul: I first learned game development with Unity, around 2020, mostly with Brackeys’ tutorials. I learned about Godot through game jams, as I’ve seen quite a few games made with it back then but I didn’t look into it at that time. What made me switch to it was that Wild Wits was using it for Aetheris, so we can say I switched to Godot because of a job opportunity. Which wasn’t that common back in 2022!

Lisa: I was first introduced to Godot during my computer science studies, and I later used it for game jams at the same school. I immediately found it very intuitive, and GDScript was also quite easy to pick up. I was also instantly charmed by its goofy little robot logo.

What do you like about Godot?

Paul: It’s easy to use, it’s open source, we own what we make with it. But mostly I think that I really enjoy the community around Godot. When I started with Unity, I loved to see that many creators making tutorials and all the activity on the forums. With Godot, I’m finding that energy again. I really like the idea of an engine made by the community that is friendly for beginners but at the same time is very good for professionals too.

Lisa: It’s open source and really easy to get the hang of!

While making your game, were there any features that you would have liked to see in Godot?

Paul: I must admit that there is only one thing I still miss from my days on Unity, and it’s the possibility to have multiple files systems and inspectors tabs and locking them. I’d love to see it on Godot one day!

What advice would you give to aspiring game developers who are just starting out in the field?

Paul: First, if you haven’t, try to do at least one game jam. You can find online game jams almost every week on itch.io and it will confront you to some of the various challenges of video game development, especially finishing a project. It’s a good way to know if you’ll enjoy game dev or not. A second advice I would give is don’t let impostor syndrome prevent you from grabbing a serious opportunity if it presents itself. The industry is in a dire state currently, and finding a place in it requires having some skills, of course, but it also requires being lucky. I was. So when a chance comes up, don’t let it slip! I’ll just assume that you should follow this advice only if you don’t endanger yourself financially. Also if you want to work in indie game dev, accept to work on different domains at once. When you are a team of four or five people making a game, you can’t expect to only do one thing, so try to be what the project might need, not only what you have on your diploma.

Lisa: I’d encourage you to take risks and try things that are a bit daring, because I think creativity is never at its best until it ends up surprising even ourselves. As Paul mentioned, game jams are incredible opportunities for experimentation in this regard, and I think it’s also important to make the most of them to occasionally create situations that take us completely out of our comfort zone and to broaden our sources of inspiration and references. You might end up creating something that feels truly your own.

Thank you very much Paul and Lisa for taking the time to answer our questions, and we look forward to see what you do next with Godot!

If you want to play Sovereign Tower, it is available on Steam for Windows and Linux.

entry.title: Dev snapshot: Godot 4.8 beta 2
entry.summary: 4.8's second beta snapshot arrives
entry.content:
In the two weeks since the release of 4.8 beta 1, our team has made great strides in ensuring the resolution of nearly 150 bugs including around 30 regressions. This blog post covering the beta snapshot, and however many more are to come, will be lighter than the dev snapshots as 4.8 is considered feature-complete at this stage. Nonetheless, there’s still a fair bit to test, so we welcome you to try our newest release for yourself: Godot 4.8 beta 2.

Please consider supporting the project financially, if you are able. Godot is maintained by the efforts of volunteers and a small team of paid contributors. Your donations go towards sponsoring their work and ensuring they can dedicate their undivided attention to the needs of the project.

Jump to the Downloads section, and give it a spin right now, or continue reading to learn more about improvements in this release. You can also try the Web editor, the XR editor, or the Android editor for this release. If you are interested in the latter, please request to join our testing group to get access to pre-release builds.

The cover illustration is from Heartfall — A Tale in Three Lives, a visual novel where you wake up as Grian on a mysterious island, and embark on an adventure with 12+ other characters partaking in fatal-but-temporary shenanigans across multiple story routes. You can buy the game on Steam, and check out the developer on Bluesky, Tumblr, and YouTube!

Highlights

For an overview of what’s new overall in Godot 4.8, have a look at the highlights for 4.8 beta 1, which cover a lot of the changes. This blog post only covers the changes between beta 1 and beta 2. This section covers the most relevant changes made since the beta 1 snapshot, which are largely regression fixes:

  • Animation: Fix collapsing the time of a bezier track with box scaling creates incorrect undo data (GH-124433).
  • Assetlib: Set the Asset Store’s default sorting back to most relevant (GH-124749).
  • Buildsystem: CI: Bump minimum Python version (3.9 → 3.10) (GH-122597).
  • C#: Enable Optimize for GodotSharp Debug builds (GH-124391).
  • Core: Nest Instruments signpost zones under a single interval name (GH-124831).
  • Editor: Disable CanvasItem manipulation for native debug builds (GH-124549).
  • Editor: Fix evaluator does not run inside static functions (GH-107791).
  • GDScript: Apply COMPLETION_DECLARATION to for variables (GH-124885).
  • GUI: BaseButton: Check visible viewport rect when handling touch events (GH-123008).
  • Import: Fix bug in insertion of lightmap caches into unwrap_cache (GH-122494).
  • Particles: Change default curve range for particle angles to [-1, 1] (GH-123959).
  • Rendering: Fix multiply blending being too dark in Compatibility (GH-124838).
  • Thirdparty: Update various Unicode-related files to version 18.0.0 (GH-123567).
  • XR: Improve error message when using a Camera3D on an XR viewport (GH-124680).

Changelog

59 contributors submitted 144 fixes for this release. See our interactive changelog for the complete list of changes since 4.8-beta1. You can also review all changes included in 4.8 compared to the previous 4.7 feature release.

While engine maintainers try their best to ensure that each preview snapshot and release candidate is stable, this is by definition a pre-release piece of software. Be sure to make frequent backups, or use a version control system such as Git, to preserve your projects in case of corruption or data loss.

Known issues

During the beta stage, we focus on solving both regressions (i.e. something that worked in a previous release is now broken) and significant new bugs introduced by new features. You can have a look at our current list of regressions and significant issues which we aim to address before releasing 4.8. This list is dynamic and will be updated if we discover new showstopping issues after more users start testing the beta snapshots.

With every release, we accept that there are going to be various issues which have already been reported but haven’t been fixed yet. See the GitHub issue tracker for a complete list of known bugs.

Bug reports

As a tester, we encourage you to open bug reports if you experience issues with this release. Please check the existing issues on GitHub first, using the search function with relevant keywords, to ensure that the bug you experience is not already known.

In particular, any change that would cause a regression in your projects is very important to report (e.g. if something that worked fine in previous 4.x releases, but no longer works in this snapshot).

Support

A big thank you to everyone who has contributed their time or their financial support to the project!

entry.title: Ready for XREAL AURA
entry.summary: Godot is part of the launch lineup for XREAL AURA
entry.content:
XREAL AURA, the first optical see-through glasses on Android XR, is here and Godot is part of the launch lineup!

Develop natively on spatial computing glasses

Download the Godot editor and its companion app on the XREAL AURA, and develop, export, and publish spatial Godot games and apps natively on XREAL AURA.
The Godot editor on XREAL AURA provides the features that you’d come to expect and love on desktop within a multi-window spatial workspace that goes with you.

Download Godot editor on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.godotengine.editor.v4

Build spatial games and apps

Godot continues the trend of being one of the lightest, most flexible, and best engines for XR development by delivering a plethora of new features to provide developers access to the newest Android XR capabilities available on XREAL AURA.

This includes support for the new OpenXR Spatial Containers, which are system-managed volumes in which applications can display spatial content, similar to how traditional applications draw 2D content within windows on a desktop.

On XREAL AURA, Godot spatial games and apps come alive right on your table, anchored exactly where you place it, with hand tracking and a low-latency spatial display that make every move feel natural.

These new spatial capabilities lower the barrier of entry for developers to build new spatial games and apps, or port existing 3D games.

Porting DOGWALK to XREAL AURA

To showcase the new OpenXR Spatial Containers on XREAL AURA, and the ease through which developers can port their 3D games to Spatial Containers, the Godot Foundation in partnership with Blender Studio and W4 Games, is working on a spatial port of DOGWALK to XREAL AURA.

This project builds on the ongoing collaboration between the Godot Foundation and W4 Games to expand Godot’s Android XR support. Working closely together, the teams have tackled the engineering challenges and optimizations involved in bringing the spatial version of DOGWALK to XREAL AURA in a relatively short time, and are now hard at work polishing the game for a release later this year. Stay tuned!

entry.title: Godot XR Community Game Jam VI
entry.summary: Results of the sixth Godot XR Community Game Jam.
entry.content:
The sixth Godot XR Community Game Jam ran from 21 September 2026 until 5 October 2026. We had 85 participants join, who submitted 28 games. Down from 98 participants but up from 22 games last jam. The quality of the entries however has risen sharply.

The theme of this game jam was “Adrift”.

The whole top 10 is worth checking out and even beyond are some real gems, but as always we’re counting down the top 5:

No 5. Balloon Dino Death Dome by Kimau

This entry has you take control of a balloon where you physically need to pull on levers to control the balloon. Well, for as far as you have control because for the most part, different air currents take over. Those air currents are brilliantly visualised and animated with tiny particles. A cannon mounted on the balloon has you shooting targets to score points.

No 4. Tether Charge Express VR by UltraGravityLabs

This entry has you trying to stay in front of a storm. Through a unique control mechanism, you control a drone on the end of a tether that gathers electricity from the storm to power your craft. It becomes a balancing act between collecting energy, evading the storm, and recharging your craft.

No 3. Build a Lighthouse VR by Bauxite

This entry is a very impressive physics-based tower stacking game. You find yourself on a little island in the middle of an ocean, with all sorts of flotsam drifting ashore. As you do, you pick up the flotsam, and try and build the highest tower. The physics interaction in this game is sublime; it is a real challenge building a tower where every new piece can upset the balance. This is hours of fun!

No 2. Balloons Adrift VR by simenhs

This deceptively simple entry has you shooting balloons out of the air. Gunplay in VR is always satisfying but what sets this apart is that at the start of the game, you only get a few seconds to shoot. With each balloon successfully popped, you get a few dollars to spend. After each round, you can buy upgrades, be it additional time, more dollars per balloon popped, more capacity in your weapon, etc. The time limit gives a sense of urgency, while the upgrade path adds an element of strategy. This is an endlessly replayable game.

No 1. Wavemaker by Unit327

Who as a kid hasn’t played endlessly in the local pool or in your bath making waves and seeing what happens? Wavemaker is an immensly satisfying entry where find yourself in a pool making waves in order to push little boats through a goal. Whether you splash with your hands, throw a plushy around, or in later levels, zoom around with a remote controlled speedboat, you make waves to manipulate the game and play through increasingly more difficult levels. This entry puts a smile on your face from the moment it starts.

Many thanks to everyone who competed and voted. It has been really great trying out all these entries. Congratulations to Unit327 for taking the win — you were up against some steep competition!

Our next game jam is pencilled in for early April 2027. We will announce an exact date closer to the jam.

entry.title: Dev snapshot: Godot 4.8 beta 1
entry.summary: Godot 4.8 enters beta!
entry.content:
It’s that time of the release cycle once again: the beta snapshot! With this, 4.8 is fully in feature-freeze, and developer resources have shifted exclusively to creating and reviewing various regression fixes.

For those interested in aiding us on our quest to squash any bugs that come up during this time, we once again encourage you to join our bug-hunting sprints. Anyone interested should read the Bug Triage Introduction for more information, and join the #bugsquad and #bugsquad-sprints channels on our developer RocketChat to participate.

Please consider supporting the project financially, if you are able. Godot is maintained by the efforts of volunteers and a small team of paid contributors. Your donations go towards sponsoring their work and ensuring they can dedicate their undivided attention to the needs of the project.

Jump to the Downloads section, and give it a spin right now, or continue reading to learn more about improvements in this release. You can also try the Web editor, the XR editor, or the Android editor for this release. If you are interested in the latter, please request to join our testing group to get access to pre-release builds.

The cover illustration is from Rita, a puzzle game with platforming elements, featuring a wide variety of word puzzles within a cozy world. You can buy the game on Steam, and follow the developer on Bluesky, YouTube, and itch.io.

Highlights

For those who have been following our development snapshots closely, you may be familiar with a number of the highlights in this post which were already covered in previous articles (4.8 dev 1, 4.8 dev 2, 4.8 dev 3, 4.8 dev 4, 4.8 dev 5, 4.8 dev 6, and 4.8 dev 7).

Because we’re already in feature freeze, there are no new features to cover compared to dev 7. Instead, we’ll focus on a general round-up of what to expect from Godot 4.8 as a whole, as well as expanding on some additions that we didn’t have the chance to highlight in our previous snapshots.

  • Breaking changes
  • 3D
  • Core
  • Documentation
  • Editor
  • GDScript
  • GUI
  • Input
  • Physics
  • Platforms
  • Rendering and shaders
  • Shaders
  • XR

Breaking changes

We try to minimize breaking changes, but sometimes they are necessary in order to fix high-priority issues. Where we do break compatibility, we do our best to make sure that the changes are minimal and require few changes in user projects.

You can find a list of such issues by filtering the merged PRs in the 4.8 milestone with the breaks compat label.

  • 3D: Remove undocumented script only enter_world callbacks (GH-111504).
  • Animation: Fix LookAtModifier3D.is_interpolating() value is inverted (GH-121391).
  • Animation: Make Bone Follower classes’ FTI off as default, add warning (GH-119509).
  • Core: Fail when trying to use local debugger in release exports (GH-122213).
  • Editor: Fix corner cases related to scroll hints across the editor (GH-117080).
  • Editor: Remove ScriptServer fallbacks from ClassDB (GH-123379).
  • Export: Do not serialize export options that do not have the PROPERTY_USAGE_STORAGE flag (GH-120721).
  • GDScript: Forbid scripts from inheriting their own inner classes (GH-121171).
  • GUI: Fix duplicated button press event on touch input (GH-120864).
  • GUI: Rework dialog default titles (GH-105550).
  • Input: Ignore joypads on unfocused window by default for new projects (GH-120399).
  • Network: mbedTLS: Update to 4.1.0, PSA Crypto (GH-120725).
  • Platforms: Android: Make OS.alert() blocking (GH-120800).
  • Rendering: Add support for ASTC 6x6 and high quality compression profiles (GH-115003).
  • Rendering: Fix sky shader SCREEN_UV builtin in Compatibility renderer (GH-121676).
  • XR: OpenXR use proper spatial entity NULL constant (GH-121815).

3D

QbieShay starts our feature round-up strong with Trail3D. Introduced in GH-117107 and built off the foundation by Zi Ye’s Cozy Cube Godot Addons, this native solution enables those seeking stunning visual effects through trails to no longer require deep knowledge of how meshes are drawn, UVs are assigned, or anything of the sort; everything Just Works™.

While being more of an editor feature, the 3D Viewport override functionality by Michael Alexsander in GH-117569 warrants a highlight in this section. Through the new editor option “Allow Viewport Override” (enabled by default), hovering the mouse over a viewport set to a specific side will cause the currently edited axis to match that side.

And more:

  • Add octant visualization to GridMap (GH-118583).
  • 3D: Re-enable freelook inertia by default in the 3D editor (GH-121478).

Core

Adam Johnston brought us “Fuzzy searching” with GH-98278, enabling search results to return matches similar to the passed query, rather than only returning an exact match. Now with GH-107126, this functionality is finally ready to roll for all users.

var items := ["Potion of Healing", "Greater Health Potion", "Poison Vial"]
var fuzzy := FuzzySearch.new()
for result in fuzzy.search_all("health potion", items):
# Prints "Greater Health Potion", "Potion of Healing".
print(result.target)

Those using version control will be thrilled to hear that serialization of objects has become much cleaner starting with GH-92102. Robert Wallis ensures that all objects are now formatted such that they won’t cause oversized diffs.

Before After

And more:

  • Core: Add support for metadata in text scenes (GH-121920).
  • Core: Introduce Variant.to<Type>() as a replacement to implicit conversions from Variant (GH-123600).
  • Core: Make it impossible to have more than one main thread, and don’t release unnecessarily (GH-121161).
  • Core: Move property maps from ClassDB to GDType. Accelerate Object property access 1.6x (GH-122596).
  • Core: Simplify GDType by storing all properties in a single unified map. Save ~12mb runtime RAM (GH-122751).
  • Core: Speed up removing many child nodes (GH-120942).

Documentation

Cyril Bissey’s efforts in GH-111375 grants our documentation—both in-editor and online—native support for admonitions; That being: the built-in systems many documentation tools provide to highlight crucial information. As time of writing, our documentation tools use simple prefixes like “Note:” or “Warning:” to convey a similar effect, but this method causes critical details to blend in with the rest of the text. So starting now, we’ll begin slowly rolling out admonition replacements for these legacy systems, which will end up looking something like what you see below:

Dark Mode Light Mode

Editor

Ever since the introduction of the EditorDock in Godot 4.6, Tomasz Chabora has been on a journey to migrate our existing editor plugins to this new system. The most ambitious migration yet occurred with GH-113051, which converts the main screen itself into a dock. This is a very fundamental change to how the editor is handled, but the benefits that are immediately available are more than worth it.

As a result of these changes:

  • The main screen editors aren’t tied to specific plugins anymore, instead being regular EditorDocks.
  • Main screen docks have their own editor setting for tab style.
  • All main screens can be closed.
  • All main screens can float.
    • The only exception is Game, as custom behavior is currently tightly integrated with WindowWrapper.

Complimenting the new structure of our editor are new and improved toolbars for our various main screens. Jayden Sipe delivered three fantastic overhauls to the Game, 2D, and 3D panels with GH-118664, GH-121080, and GH-121065 respectively. All three being spearheaded by the same creative vision ensures a uniform style; one which heavily emphasizes usability and clarity in comparison to the prior implementations.

  Before After
Game
2D
3D

Mikael Hermansson delivers the ability to drag-toggle visibility in the scene tree editor with GH-118634. Now when toggling the visibility of a given node, the newly toggled state can be applied to any subsequent nodes when dragging the mouse across them.

It’s never been easier to make a title more accessible to users across multiple languages, thanks to the use of pseudolocalization. Tomasz Chabora, seeking to further expand the utility and awareness of our language hot-swap functionality, enabled pseudolocalization within the editor itself in GH-119443. This simple toggle simulates changes that might take place during localization, allowing any issues that would come from that process to be recognized as early as possible in development.

Hugo Locurcio’s work in GH-99725 brought a long-desired QOL addition to the inspector: auto-expansion of resources. While most of our inspector items automatically revealed themselves when initialized, resources always existed as an unfortunate blindspot. As demonstrated below, this will no longer be the case!

DexterFstone made it possible to play a scene from the file system directly in GH-111941. Now any scene can be played from the file system’s context menu alone; no extra steps required!

Jayden returns with two more editor goodies in GH-119103, aiming to expand the QOL for our FileSystem logic. The first of these features is the ability to zoom in/out of the window with a mouse’s scrollwheel. By simply holding Ctrl while hovering over a FileSystem window, the contents will either grow or shrink upon scrolling the mouse up or down respectively.

Next up is glob-based searching. Sometimes you want to find a type of file or something with a specific prefix, without necessarily narrowing it down to a specific file. By utilizing glob-based search, now your results can explicitly capture whatever use-case you desire.

Michael Alexsander keeps the editor train rolling with another highly-requested feature: runtime manipulation of CanvasItems! Thanks to his work in GH-122510, the following functionality is now fully integrated within Godot 4.8 (lifted verbatim from the original PR):

  • Movement, resizing, rotation, scaling, and pivot modification of CanvasItems, together with its own toolbar.
  • Full undo/redo support, unified in the editor’s undo/redo manager.
  • Added the ability to open scenes by double-clicking them in the game. Just like how it’s done in the editor.
  • Improved remote shortcut handling. Which is now funneled into a single debugger message, and triggers the pressed visual on the buttons.
  • Improved mouse cursor updates in the editor. Now they trigger immediately rather than after an action is taken with the mouse again.

We’ll end our editor highlights with symbol renaming, an experimental feature brought to us by Tomasz with GH-117949. With this, renaming a symbol will properly propogate that logic across the project, uniformly applying the rename where relevant.

And more:

  • Add an option to run the project upgrade tool when updating to a new Godot version (GH-119466).
  • Add Clear Project Cache option (GH-120093).
  • Add replace preview to Find in Files (GH-122659).
  • Add toggle button for texture preview metadata overlay (GH-117216).
  • Automatically create default resources in the editor for many objects (GH-88647).
  • Clean and simplify Inspector header (GH-117499).
  • Embed the game view in the main editor window as the default (GH-120736).
  • Fix metadata formatting in inspector (GH-108878).
  • List monitor resolutions and refresh rates in editor Copy System Info (GH-122809).
  • Make main screen dock colors more readable (GH-122903).
  • Show doc tooltips in quick settings (GH-121278).
  • Show enum integer values in inspector tooltips (GH-102734).
  • Show inspector warning on deprecated properties (GH-121364).
  • Turn the script method outline into a Tree (GH-121534).
  • Use VHS Circle as the default editor color picker shape (GH-110615).

GDScript

Courtesy of Malcolm Anderson in GH-119588, the debugging process for GDScript will become much more streamlined thanks to the direct and immediate information provided by underlined warnings. While you would previously have a line with a warning/error be highlighted if a problem existed, it highlighted the entire line, which both obfuscated the problem and risked multiple issues being hidden if they existed on the same line. With these changes, only the relevant portions of a given line will be underlined. For instance, the following codeblock would’ve previously been highlighted in its entirety:

And more:

  • Disallow strings as comments (GH-121833).
  • Fix shutdown crash when ScriptInstance references its owner (GH-121762).
  • Improve performance for Syntax Highlighting (GH-123320).
  • Make language shutdown more crash resilient (GH-120976).

GUI

Every developer knows the struggle of text container constraints all too well. No matter how reasonable you think your font scale is, or what kind of variable text you believe can make it in, a translation string or player input will inevitably break those bounds. Even if you actively and thoroughly filter all input length at all times, that’s still a lot of code upkeep and boilerplating across different areas of your project to achieve the desired effect.

Ismail Ivanov is one of many who felt this struggle of our text container constraints, and decided to do something about it. GH-116791 grants Label and RichTextLabel resize-to-fit functionality, utilizing three newly-added properties: auto_font_size, min_font_size, and max_font_size.

One of the most common requests we’ve seen for improving Tree functionality is the ability to support “sticky items”. That is: the ability for a given line to stick to the top if it represents a foldable region. Koliur Rahman is no stranger to integrating popular editor requests, so it was only a matter of time before they delivered the desired functionality in GH-115697.

And more:

  • Add format property to SpinBox and deprecate prefix/suffix (GH-103998).
  • Add new default algorithm of automatic focus strategy for Control nodes (GH-120631).
  • Audio: Add theme sound items and playback on common UI events (GH-111455).
  • TabBar: Add options for tab sizing strategy (GH-113385).
  • Use OS taskbar progress when ProgressDialog is shown (GH-121505).

Input

Many of our existing GUI items have received native touch support in 4.8, warranting a separate input-focused section dedicated to showcasing their new functionality. All of the following featured items come courtesy of Anish Kumar.

Starting with GH-119706’s two-for-one package deal, both TextEdit and CodeEdit received the following new functionality:

  • Tap (press → release): Positions the cursor and opens the virtual keyboard.
  • Drag (press → drag → release): scrolls the text content, including inertial scrolling support.
    • This extends to the code completion popup, which previously could not be scrolled via touch input.
  • Text selection:
    • Double-tap selects a word.
    • Double-tap, hold, and drag selects the portion you’re hovering over.

TabBar received similar treatment, and is especially easy to showcase thanks to the main screen’s recent conversion to docks, though this functionality will be available to any and all TabBar instances.

PopupMenu is similarly simple to convey through the editor, and is equally available to any and all instances of PopupMenu.

Physics

aterray, in collaboration with Ricardo Buring and Mikael Hermansson, implemented non-allocating classes for PhysicsDirectSpaceState2D and PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D in GH-113970. By leveraging these new methods, result objects can be successfully reused to avoid unnecessary dictionary and array allocations on every call.

var result := PhysicsCastMotionResult3D.new()
func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
if direct_space_state.cast_motion_into(params, result):
...

These new objects are strongly typed, meaning the need for manual type declarations and dictionary lookups are no longer required.

# Old implementation:
var dict := direct_space_state.intersect_ray(params)
if dict:
# Cannot infer the type of "normal"
# var normal := dict["normal"]
var normal: Vector3 = dict["normal"]
# New implementation:
var result := PhysicsIntersectRayResult3D.new()
if direct_space_state.intersect_ray_into(params, result):
var normal := result.get_normal() # Inferred as Vector3.
var position := result.get_position() # Inferred as Vector3.

  • Add get_velocity_at_(local)_position() to RigidBody2D (GH-121142) and RigidBody3D (GH-121122).

While Godot supports exporting projects to Android, we sympathize with those developers who’ve struggled with the busywork that comes with it. That is: handling the SDK setup for Android and Java beforehand. Nobody is more familiar with this workflow than Fredia Huya-Kouadio, which is why he took to streamlining the entire process in GH-121849. Now, at the click of a button, the editor will take care of downloading, setting up, and managing the Android and Java SDKs automatically!

And more:

  • Editor: Enable screen orientation change on large screens and in Project Manager (GH-121387).
  • Editor: Update game menu bar to match desktop editor (GH-119156).
  • Implement OS::get_processor_name() for Android (GH-120896).

macOS

Starting with 4.8 beta 1, macOS binaries will be distributed as separate architectures. This is thanks to bruvzg introducing the concept in GH-123112, enabling the binaries that we distribute to be much more compact by default. The option for universal packages still exists and functions as it always has, but for the sake of streamlining our outputs and keeping in-line with the amount of size reduction efforts that’ve occurred this cycle, we’ll be moving forward with the individual architectures as our default for official distribution.

And more:

  • Export: macOS: Add architecture selector to the export options (GH-119708).
  • Force reset main menu on app activation (GH-124172).
  • Input: Fix removal of last key down event before IME activation (GH-122799).

Windows

We recently released a dedicated blog post that goes into detail on how we fixed high polling rate mice on Windows in Godot. Those wanting a deeper dive are encouraged to read the changes for themselves, though the improvements speak for themselves:

Before After

And more:

  • Implement support for desktop toast notifications (no WinRT/C++) (GH-121711).
  • Replace WinRT/C++ dependency with custom COM+ code (GH-121633).

Rendering and shaders

KenzieMac130 starts out our rendering highlights strong with an incredibly impressive first-time contribution in GH-115426, which introduces multi-bounce ambient occlusion approximation. Previously, ambient occlusion in Godot failed to account for interreflections, meaning scenes were over-darkened in practice. Moving forward, we’ll be able to leverage a low-cost approximation of these interreflections, providing a more vibrant and accurate representation of what a given surface “should” look like.

As cited in the PR, this implementation is based upon a method from this 2016 Siggraph presentation, the technique of which has been adoped as industry-standard across multiple other engines. Those seeking a more technical breakdown are strongly encouraged to view the presentation itself!

Disabled Enabled

Much like the previous point, Juan Manuel builds upon an existing foundation—this time by longtime member Hugo Locurcio—in order to introduce directional lightmap specular light to the engine with GH-109737. This addresses an existing issue with the way baked directional light set as static interacted with the LightmapGI set to directional, as this combination failed to bake any specular information. Thanks to the aforementioned PR, any directional specular information can not only be baked into the LightmapGI, but will produce results comparable to realtime directional light!

Those who want more a more technical breakdown on the subject are encouraged to watch this 2018 GDC presentation. For practical examples, we welcome you to enjoy this small sample of comparisons pulled from the PR:

Disabled Enabled

In the context of an engine such as Godot, “texture streaming” refers to the ability to dynamically load and unload images based on a camera’s relative position. Such a system would allow games to handle significantly more visible textures at any given point in time, which is why such a feature was one of the community’s most desired. Unfortunately, like most highly-desired features, it’s much easier said than done, and the “best” implementation direction isn’t exactly set in stone.

The approach that Trevor Davenport took in GH-113429 was mip-level texture streaming. That is: Godot now only loads the necessary mipmap of a texture, representing smaller or less detailed versions of the base texture when far away or otherwise obfuscated. This results in a significant reduction of VRAM requirements for textures, particularly for 3D titles with large, open worlds.

Speaking of mipmaps: an existing issue in the engine was actually caused by their use, albeit indirectly. Certain material shaders, such as alpha scissor, would look pretty rough at long distances; this was a direct result of mipmap levels causing them to overfilter and dissolve away. While technical workarounds do exist, such as using a texture format with built-in alpha coverage like .dds, it’s still too much of a technical hurdle for what should be straightforward.

Kasper Arnklit Frandsen shared the above sentiment, leading him to create GH-104289. This allows any given texture to preserve their alpha data, even when falling back to their scaled-down equivalents.

Rudolph Bester ended up using Bend Studios’ approach in his implementation with GH-118045. With these changes, a new option has been added to the environment resource and directional light node to enable screen space contact shadows (SSCS). It creates an R8 shadow texture for each directional light in the scene and blends them with existing shadow maps. This results in performant shadows that don’t compromise their visual quality.

Disabled Enabled

While our decals have gotten some attention this development cycle, perhaps the most stand-out addition comes at the hands of Colin O’Rourke. Being the brain behind DrawableTexture, it should come as no surprise that he managed to wrangle them once again with GH-115653, enabling decals to be fully animated.

And more:

  • Add decal support to compatibility renderer (GH-118070).
  • Add support for ASTC 6x6 and high quality compression profiles (GH-115003).
  • Fix directional shadow culling for orthogonal cameras (GH-121775).
  • Improve SPIR-V reflection performance (GH-121835).
  • Use non-volumetric fog in WorldEnvironment sky reflections (GH-107958).

Shaders

While we’re quite happy with the current state of our visual shader, some pain points have always remained. This is especially true for more complex implementations, as the scope of the graphs could become quite unwieldy over time. It’s no surprise then, that one of the most common requests for the visual shader was a way to reduce or remove the bloat and redundancy that comes from these complex files.

Hendrik Brucker delivered a solution in GH-99404, gracing the visual shader with the versatility and ubiquity of node groups. By leveraging node groups, users can now efficiently encapsulate frequently-used sections of a shader and reuse them across the graph with zero friction. What was once a chaotic mess of boilerplate and difficult-to-parse information is now neatly bundled with dedicated node groups:

And more:

  • GDShader: Add implicit conversion of bool constants to float, int, and uint (GH-120715).

XR

Remember Ricardo Sanchez-Saez, the contributor responsible for native visionOS support? Well, their work hasn’t concluded just yet, as they—along with co-authors Stuart Carnie and huiedenanhai—bring visionOS to new life as a module in GH-109975! With these changes, not only has our build server’s logic dramatically simplified, but this lays the groundwork for tvOS support in the near-future!

When first announced, we promised more information coming soon™, and that promise stands. It’ll be a little while longer still, so we thank you for your patience!

And more:

  • visionOS: Add support for hand tracking and PSVR2 controllers on Apple Vision Pro (GH-122567).

entry.summary: Feature freeze has arrived!
entry.content:
It’s that time once again: feature freeze! With this, no new features will be integrated for Godot 4.8 moving forward, and priorities will be shifting exclusively towards bugfixes and addressing regressions to ensure a functional baseline as soon as possible. So join us for one last round-up of features, as we prepare for the beta transition!

Please consider supporting the project financially, if you are able. Godot is maintained by the efforts of volunteers and a small team of paid contributors. Your donations go towards sponsoring their work and ensuring they can dedicate their undivided attention to the needs of the project.

Jump to the Downloads section, and give it a spin right now, or continue reading to learn more about improvements in this release. You can also try the Web editor, the XR editor, or the Android editor for this release. If you are interested in the latter, please request to join our testing group to get access to pre-release builds.

The cover illustration is from 20 More, Somehow Even Smaller, Mazes, a successor to 20 Small Mazes, featuring 20 more mazes that’re somehow even smaller. You can get the game for free on Steam, and follow the developer on YouTube or Bluesky.

Highlights

In case you missed them, see the 4.8 dev 1, 4.8 dev 2, 4.8 dev 3, 4.8 dev 4, 4.8 dev 5, and 4.8 dev 6 release notes for an overview of some key features which were already in those snapshots, and are therefore still available for testing in 4.8 dev 7.

Editor: Symbol renaming

Tomasz Chabora has been hard at work in the editor throught the entirety of Godot 4.8’s development, and is going out with a bang with GH-117949 introducing symbol renaming! This has consistently hovered around the top of the list for most-requested features for multiple years now, and managed to squeeze in at the very last second before feature freeze set in. With this, renaming a symbol will properly propogate that logic across the project, uniformly applying the rename where relevant.

Here’s the tool differentiating a class identifier from a comment and string:

Here’s the tool differentiating local variables which share the same name across different methods:

As this was such a last-second addition, the feature is currently marked as “experimental” and temporarily requires an opt-in. While we’re reasonably confident in the implementation as it stands, we wanted a few extra precautions to ensure that users could try this without having to wait for Godot 4.9 or later.

Editor: Game view CanvasItem manipulation

Michael Alexsander keeps the editor train rolling with another highly-requested feature: runtime manipulation of CanvasItems! Thanks to his work in GH-122510, the following functionality is now fully integrated within Godot 4.8 (lifted verbatim from the original PR):

  • Movement, resizing, rotation, scaling, and pivot modification of CanvasItems, together with its own toolbar.
  • Full undo/redo support, unified in the editor’s undo/redo manager.
  • Added the ability to open scenes by double-clicking them in the game. Just like how it’s done in the editor.
  • Improved remote shortcut handling. Which is now funneled into a single debugger message, and triggers the pressed visual on the buttons.
  • Improved mouse cursor updates in the editor. Now they trigger immediately rather than after an action is taken with the mouse again.

Rendering: Animated decals

While our decals have gotten some attention this development cycle, perhaps the most stand-out addition comes at the hands of Colin O’Rourke. Being the brain behind DrawableTexture, it should come as no surprise that he managed to wrangle them once again with GH-115653, enabling decals to be fully animated.

Physics: Add non-allocating query methods for PhysicsDirectSpaceState2D/3D

Those of you who’ve been following Godot since 4.0 dropped might be familiar with this zero allocation API proposal by Juan Linietsky, in which he highlighted some potential avenues for alleviating allocations in our bindings. While we’ve since taken several steps towards improving performance and resolving unnecessary allocations internally, the core of the issue persists even now. While foundational changes will be necessary to truly do away with the issue, we’re able to significantly mitigate these concerns by introducing classes which act as a middle-man of sorts, preventing unnecessary allocations and preserving type hints.

Enter aterray, who collaborated with Ricardo Buring and Mikael Hermansson to implement several such classes in GH-113970 for PhysicsDirectSpaceState2D and PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D. By leveraging these new methods, result objects can be successfully reused to avoid unnecessary dictionary and array allocations on every call.

var result := PhysicsCastMotionResult3D.new()
func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
if direct_space_state.cast_motion_into(params, result):
...

As previously mentioned, these new objects are strongly typed. As such, the need for manual type declarations and dictionary lookups are no longer required.

# Old implementation:
var dict := direct_space_state.intersect_ray(params)
if dict:
# Cannot infer the type of "normal"
# var normal := dict["normal"]
var normal: Vector3 = dict["normal"]
# New implementation:
var result := PhysicsIntersectRayResult3D.new()
if direct_space_state.intersect_ray_into(params, result):
var normal := result.get_normal() # Inferred as Vector3.
var position := result.get_position() # Inferred as Vector3.

GUI: Native touch support for TabBar and PopupMenu

GUI fans rejoice, as you’re getting two lovely GUI additions in Godot 4.8, courtesy of Anish Kumar. These additions are in the form of fully-native touch support for TabBar (GH-122960) and PopupMenu (GH-123576), delivering some excellent quality-of-life for our users and developers on touch-based devices.

The additions to TabBar are especially easy to showcase thanks to the main screen’s recent conversion to docks, but this functionality will be available to any and all TabBar instances.

PopupMenu is similarly simple to convey through the editor, and is equally available to any and all instances of PopupMenu.

The large scrollbar shown in the video is specific to the editor, serving as a vestige of pre-touch functionality. Its size will be reduced in the near future.

Audio: Add theme sound items and playback on common UI events

Hugo Locurcio continues to give GUIs some love with GH-111455, bringing proper audio functionality to many of those elements. Now developers can take advantage of sound events to trigger audio effects on-command with the new “audio” theme item type, including the ability to alter them with the theme override system.

Currently, custom controls cannot play theme audio items. This will be rectified by GH-123867, slated for integration shortly after 4.8 dev 7 releases.

Platforms: AccessKit for iOS and Android

Godot 4.5 saw the integration of screen reader support for desktop platforms. This was thanks to the wonderful UI utility AccessKit, providing a reliable infrastructure for accessibility options. The reason it was limited to desktop platforms at the time came down to the logistics of the API and not wanting to keep accessibility options locked-off while other platforms were resolved. However, we never stopped pursuing its integration across other platforms; after all:

Accessibility should be every developer’s top priority, full-stop.

That’s why we’re thrilled to announce that two major platforms will be gaining native AccessKit support: iOS and Android! The former is brought to us by first-time contributor Ben Humphries in GH-119750, while the latter is provided by our primary AccessKit maintainer bruvzg in GH-117785. While the amount of features on offer for these devices might not be on the same level as their desktop equivalents, the door is now wide-open for further improvements, so we eagerly await everyone’s testing and feedback!

The AcccessKit iOS implementation still has some inherent limitations, such as a lack of support for editable text fields. Progress on this can be tracked on this issue in the AccessKit repository.

  • C#: Upgrade packages and minimum TFM required to net10.0 (GH-123738).
  • Core: Introduce Variant.to<Type>() as a replacement to implicit conversions from Variant (GH-123600).

  • Platforms: Web: Implement Web Editor debugger via MessagePort (GH-123327).

Indeed, this is much sooner than usual. entry.title: Optimizing CPU-side Rendering Code
entry.summary: Optimizing CPU code is a lot of fun. Here’s how we do it
entry.content:
I want to give people a little bit of insight into what the optimization process looks like for Godot’s renderer. From the outside, rendering optimization can look a little bit like black magic. I want to show a few examples of some optimizations that we did this year to highlight that optimizing rendering code isn’t as scary as it sounds.

Bottlenecks

In this article I will only be looking at optimizing CPU code. When working on renderers, you need to be very careful about optimizing code both for the CPU and for the GPU, because your ultimate performance will be dictated by the slower of the two processors. No amount of CPU optimization will save you from inefficient shaders.

In writing a renderer you also make tradeoffs all the time to benefit one or the other. For example, batching in 2D is a technique that hurts GPU performance a little, but improves CPU performance a lot. Since 2D games tend to get CPU bottlenecked before they get GPU bottlenecked, batching ends up being a net positive in most cases. Conversely, 3D games tend to be GPU bottlenecked more often, so in Godot we do our occlusion culling on the CPU in order to take some of the load off the GPU.

Regardless of your ultimate balance between CPU and GPU work, it is always beneficial to optimize the engine since any optimization to the engine leaves more space for game developers to use the CPU and GPU and saves battery power for power-constrained platforms.

Methodology

The process of optimizing CPU performance roughly looks like:

  1. Identify the performance bottlenecks/hotspots
  2. Understand why the bottleneck is where it is
  3. Investigate solutions
  4. Re-measure performance
  5. Repeat

Identify the performance bottlenecks

This is the hardest part of performance optimization. When your game or application starts running poorly it can be difficult to track down exactly why. Often once you see where the poor performance is coming from, you immediately understand why performance is bad. This is often the case when you accidentally call an expensive API in a hot loop, or you leave in some debug code that should never have seen the light of day.

For us, as engine developers, we have the added challenge of needing to optimize for a wide range of potential games. We don’t have just one target, we have thousands of moving targets and we only know there is a serious problem when people make bug reports. That being said, we can identify and make many improvements just testing using our existing demos and open-source games.

The best tool for identifying CPU bottlenecks is a CPU profiler. They come in many shapes and sizes. Godot even has two built into the editor (one for profiling GDScript code and another for profiling the renderer exclusively). However, when working on engine code itself, you need to use an external profiler. Godot has support for building with Tracy to do tracing profiling, but you can also use an external sampling profiler.

My tool of choice is Superluminal which is an external sampling profiler. It attaches to a running instance of Godot and records profiling data as you run the engine. Then it provides a very nice visualization of what code is running when. It also recently got Linux support! The examples below in this article will be using Superluminal.

Understand the bottleneck

As mentioned above, sometimes it is easy to understand the bottleneck. Especially when the poor performance is due to a bug and not a poor design choice. Oftentimes understanding the bottleneck requires understanding the surrounding code.

Ultimately performance optimization boils down to “don’t do things that don’t need to be done”. Understanding the code and understanding the system is very helpful to understanding what things need to be done and what things are unnecessary.

Investigate solutions

Typically, once you understand the bottleneck, the solution will seem obvious. But sometimes you need to try a few different things before you figure out exactly what is required. For example, you might see a heavy loop with a lot of calculations in it and initially think the solution is to do less calculations per iteration. But it could turn out that the problem comes from memory bandwidth, so re-structuring your data might yield better performance gains.

Ultimately, you will make changes that directly reduce the impact of the bottleneck.

Re-measure performance

You always need to re-measure. Computers are very complex, game engines are very complex, sometimes the thing you think will be faster is not faster. Optimizations are often counter-intuitive. For example, adding a branch in a for loop to skip some calculations intuitively seems like it will always be faster, but in many cases it stops the compiler from vectorizing the loop and thus leads to worse performance. Or, a more common example, you may cache a value to avoid calculating something twice, but if your bottleneck in that code path is memory reads, then caching the value will make your code slower and you would have been better off doing the work twice.

Unless you are an absolute C++ compiler genius, you likely can’t guess the exact result of your code change on performance. So it is always better to re-measure and confirm your results.

Case Study #1: Polygon2D

This PR came out of a conversation I had with Aurélien Condomines who is working on Heidi’s Legacy: Mountains Calling. He noted that he found the animation code in Godot to be very slow which was limiting his ability to add content to his game. He found that by having 20 or so animated characters, performance would start to fall off in his game.

I was surprised at those numbers and felt that something was wrong. Our animation code shouldn’t be a bottleneck with only 20 or so animated characters so I decided to investigate. I asked him to put together a minimal project with a bunch of animated sprites on screen so I could profile it.

This first hint is that he was using an AnimationPlayer to animate the vertices of a Polygon2D that was displayed on a Viewport on a Sprite3D in order to have nice looking 2D animations in a 3D world.

That alone sounds a bit unique, but it isn’t something that should cause any significant problems. So our next step is to boot up Superluminal and see what is going on.

I captured a few seconds of the demo running and then zoomed in on a frame.

Note: all testing of this demo scene is done with a Ryzen 5 9600X CPU.

Since it isn’t totally clear in the screenshot, here is a breakdown of where we are spending our time:

  • 4.6 ms: AnimationMixer. That is slower than I would like to see, but there are a lot of animation tracks in this scene since every vertex is being animated, so it isn’t totally unexpected.
  • 15.7 ms: Polygon2D::_notification(). I will say more about this below.
  • 11.7 ms: Drawing the scene. Of this 3.3 ms is spent creating vertex arrays, and 5 ms is spent freeing vertex arrays. So we only spend about 3.4 ms actually rendering the scene.

With just this high-level overview, we can immediately tell that there are two things going wrong:

  1. Polygon2D is doing something unexpected.
  2. Whatever it is, it is resulting in vertex arrays getting created and freed every frame.

So let’s take a close look and see where the time is spent in Polygon2D. We have two options, we can just zoom in on the timeline, which looks like this:

Or we can use the call graph below to get a more detailed overview:

The call graph orders the function calls inside the chosen function by how expensive they are. You can see that most of the time is spent adding a new surface and freeing the previous one. That aligns with what we already saw in the rendering code. Now we know that the Polygon2D class is responsible for the poor performance even at rendering time.

Now, we can look over at the “Source and Disassembly” panel to see exactly what lines of code are responsible:

This code is responsible for building the internal mesh for the Polygon2D. This profile is telling us that this code is running every frame and it is very slow. After putting everything together, its no surprise the mesh is being rebuilt every frame, since the vertices are changing on the CPU every frame!

Based on our profile result, we know that is a really slow process. So the question is, can we do something about it?

Of course!

Godot exposes a low-level API to manually update vertex data. This can be extremely helpful when you know the number of vertices in a mesh is going to stay the same. Instead of freeing the old mesh, allocating a new one, and then uploading the vertex data to the new mesh, we can simply upload the vertex data to the existing mesh.

That’s what I ended up doing in my pull request. Most of the work in the PR was identifying which cases were suitable for updating the mesh, and which cases needed the mesh to be recreated.

This optimization roughly tripled the performance of animated Polygon2Ds, making the technique that Aurélien was using totally viable.

Taking a look at a single frame after my PR, we have gone from 35 ms per frame to just 13 ms:

Rendering now accounts for about 50% of the frame time, animation takes about 30% and the Polygon2D update takes about 20%.

This same bit of code could be optimized much further of course. For one, we are re-uploading the entire mesh data each frame that any vertex moves. A potential optimization would be to only update the region of the mesh that changed. That way if you have an animation that only impacts a few vertices, you don’t pay the cost for the full upload.

However, such an optimization would need to be guided by a game or scene that would actually benefit from partial updates. This game basically animates every vertex every frame, so the tracking required to do partial updates would likely be a net negative. Remember, to properly optimize something you need to be able to test your optimization! If you don’t have a test case, you can’t do an optimization properly.

Ultimately, the small and safe optimization I did yielded enough performance gains to go from 28 FPS to 83 FPS on my device. So it was enough for now. If someone was really interested and had the time, performance could be pushed further. Personally, I’m most curious about where we are spending time in the rendering frame now since that accounts for 50% of the frame time.

Case Study #2: Optimizing SPIRV to DXIL Transpilation

Earlier this year, Asilkan was investigating our shader compilation pipeline on the D3D12 backend. Our current method for compiling shaders with D3D12 is described in this earlier blog post from Pedro. In short it is:

  1. Compile GDShader to GLSL using built in shader compiler
  2. Compile GLSL to SPIRV using GLSLang
  3. Transpile SPIRV to DXIL using Mesa’s NIR converter
  4. Submit DXIL to GPU driver to be compiled to binary

By far the slowest part of the process is the transpilation step. Further, it leads to a noticeable difference in loading times when switching from Vulkan to DXIL since Vulkan can use SPIRV directly.

To optimize this, Asilkan ran a trace through Superluminal and analyzed the results. From a very high level you can already see that there are significant gaps where only a couple of threads are active. Gaps in thread execution mean that things are taking longer than they theoretically should. Ideally our loading process would fully saturate all cores in order to load as fast as possible. That’s the goal anyway.

Right off the bat, you can see something is wrong. Green means the thread is doing work. The height of the green bar is basically how hard the thread is working. Red means the thread is stalled waiting for something.

The beautiful thing about a profiler like Superluminal in a situation like this is you can zoom in and see what is happening. Here, Asilkan was able to see that these gaps were all caused by threads requesting more memory from the OS. While the work was heavily multithreaded, all threads ended up waiting on each other while they waited on the OS to allocate more heap memory.

So what if we just didn’t do that?

What Asilkan ended up doing is giving each thread their own heap and getting them to allocate from that instead of frequently asking the OS for more memory from a single global heap. The end result is the threads are no longer stuck waiting for the OS and their execution now looks like:

This optimization saved 11 seconds of load time in the TPS demo. Those 11 seconds were purely wasted time where the CPU ended up stalled doing nothing.

Conclusion

I hope this post has helped show what we actually do to optimize components of the renderer. The process isn’t super complicated, especially when you have the right tools on hand. In both cases the solution was very apparent once the problem was properly identified.

Highlights

In case you missed them, see the 4.8 dev 1, 4.8 dev 2, 4.8 dev 3, and 4.8 dev 4 release notes for an overview of some key features which were already in those snapshots, and are therefore still available for testing in 4.8 dev 5.

Rendering: Mip-level texture streaming

In the context of an engine such as Godot, “texture streaming” refers to the ability to dynamically load and unload images based on a camera’s relative position. Such a system would allow games to handle significantly more visible textures at any given point in time, which is why such a feature was one of the community’s most desired. Unfortunately, like most highly-desired features, it’s much easier said than done, and the “best” implementation direction isn’t exactly set in stone.

The approach that Trevor Davenport took in GH-113429 was mip-level texture streaming. That is: Godot now only loads the necessary mipmap of a texture, representing smaller or less detailed versions of the base texture when far away or otherwise obfuscated. This results in a significant reduction of VRAM requirements for textures, particularly for 3D titles with large, open worlds.

In order to leverage this new functionality, streaming must first be enabled in the project settings, necessitating an editor restart. You can make runtime changes via the TextureStreaming singleton.

Once enabled, textures can be imported as streamed textures, utilizing the new texture import type: “Texture2D Streamed”. This new texture type comes equipped with overrides for minimum and maximum resolution for a given texture, so you can safely preserve crucial details on a case-by-case basis. The per-texture properties override the system settings; the default is to use the system settings.

Import: Allow preserving alpha test coverage

Speaking of mipmaps: an existing issue in the engine was actually caused by their use, albeit indirectly. Certain material shaders, such as alpha scissor, would look pretty rough at long distances; this was a direct result of mipmap levels causing them to overfilter and dissolve away. While technical workarounds do exist, such as using a texture format with built-in alpha coverage like .dds, it’s still too much of a technical hurdle for what should be straightforward.

Kasper Arnklit Frandsen shared the above sentiment, leading him to create GH-104289. This allows any given texture to preserve their alpha data, even when falling back to their scaled-down equivalents.

Editor: Clean and simplify 2D toolbar

Jayden Sipe rounds out our highlights this time with GH-121080, bringing the editor’s 2D toolbar a well-earned makeover. Being the same mind behind the overhaul of our game view toolbar, these changes increase parity between the docks with a consistent vision and design philosophy.
